shipped_originals.title_o: Can you say no? Examining the relationship between drinking refusal self-efficacy and protective behavioral strategy use on alcohol outcomes
Protective behavioral strategies as a mediator and moderator of the relationship between self-regulation and alcohol-related consequences in first-year college students.

blind_target.evidence_quote: We aimed to replicate and extend the findings from three published studies that have examined putative moderators of PBS-alcohol associations: self-regulation, negative urgency, and drinking refusal self-efficacy.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Although we replicated most main effects and bivariate correlations, we failed to replicate any of the moderation effects (i.e., interaction effects).
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Target is the self-regulation moderation finding. The abstract gives a set-wide failure verdict for all moderation effects, the central findings being re-tested; replicated main effects and correlations do not change this verdict. Original citation absent from abstract.

shipped_originals.title_o: Effects of an Automated Vocabulary and Comprehension Intervention
shipped_originals.authors_o: Spencer; Goldstein; Sherman; Noe; Tabbah; Ziolkowski; Schneider

blind_target.evidence_quote: In 2013, Spencer, Goldstein, Sherman, et al. reported the promising effects of a supplemental, technology-assisted, storybook intervention (Tier 2) containing embedded instruction targeting the oral language learning of preschool children at risk for delays. We sought to advance knowledge of the intervention by replicating it in a new sample and examining children’s responses to the narrator’s instructional prompts and associations with learning outcomes.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Exposure to the intervention accelerated children’s weekly oral language learning, and effect sizes were comparable to those of Spencer et al.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Abstract explicitly compares the intervention effects to Spencer et al. and reports comparable effects.

shipped_originals.title_o: Preferences, Constraints, and the Process of Sex Segregation in College Majors: A Choice Analysis

blind_target.evidence_quote: Ochsenfeld (2016) has found that a substantial part of sex segregation in higher education results from differences in vocational interests (i.e., preferences), while constraints (e.g., relative math grades) play only a minor role. We challenge the validity of these findings because earlier work employed a cross-sectional student sample and might therefore suffer from endogenous selection (i.e., post hoc rationalizations due to simultaneous reporting of majors and preferences) and postoutcome collider bias (i.e., conditioning on the outcome). Our replication study uses panel data (National Educational Panel Study, NEPS-SC4) that allow adjustment for the two sources of bias through the application of a pretransition preference measure and inverse probability weighting.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Our analyses demonstrate the validity of prior research.

blind_target.authors: Han, W., Ada, S., Sharman, R., & Rao, H. R.
blind_target.title: Campus emergency notification systems: An examination of factors affecting compliance with alerts.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
This study is a conceptual replication of the study by Han et al. (2015) in which the authors evaluated factors affecting
students’ compliance with emergency instructions during campus emergencies.
blind_target.outcome_quote:
Results obtained from the current study indicate mixed support for results from the original study. Results
from the unabridged dataset were consistent with the original study, while those from the verify-first dataset
differed.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Explicit overall mixed-support verdict: unabridged results agree while verify-first results differ.
